newsitem.title: USA: Fed expected to hold interest rates steady.
newsitem.headline: Fed expected to hold interest rates steady.

text.p: The Federal Reserve on Wednesday began a second day of deliberating interest rate policy, with most analysts expecting the central bank to leave rates unchanged.

With economic growth slowing from its sizzling first-quarter pace and inflation low and stable, analysts said Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan should have little trouble convincing fellow policy-makers to keep rates unchanged.
"There's no reason to move at this point," said David Jones, vice chairman of Wall Street broker Aubrey G. Lanston and Co.
In another sign of slowing growth, the Commerce Department reported on Wednesday that factory orders slumped 0.7 percent in May after surging 1.4 percent in April.

Bond prices edged higher and stocks marked time as investors awaited word from the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee, which was expected to announce its rate decision at about 2:15 p.m. EDT (1815 GMT).
While many analysts did not expect a rate change this week, many central bank watchers believe it is only a matter of time before the Fed raises interest rates again.

None of the 36 economists surveyed by Reuters expected the Fed to tighten credit this week, although 15 are looking for the central bank to boost rates at its next meeting, on Aug. 19. Others expect a rate increase in the fall.
"Economic activity will pick up steam in the third quarter and that will prompt the Fed to act," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist of Minneapolis-based Norwest Corp.

The Fed increased short-term rates in March for the first time in more than two years in a bid to brake the economy's growth and keep inflation from rising. The federal funds rate --the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans -- was raised a quarter percentage point to 5.5 percent.

But the central bank held off from tightening credit further at its last meeting in May, largely at the behest of Greenspan, who argued that the economy would slow on its own without another rate rise by the Fed.

That is indeed what has happened. Growth appears to have slowed to an annualized pace of between 1.5 percent and 2 percent in the second quarter from a torrid 5.9 percent rate in the first, the fastest clip in more than nine years, analysts said.
"The whole issue for both the markets and the Fed is whether the pause in second-quarter growth will persist," Lanston's Jones said.
Jones, for one, thinks it will not. He sees economic growth speeding up in the second half of the year as wage gains and the buoyant stock market fuel stepped-up consumer spending.
The economy is already running at or above capacity -- unemployment is at a 23-year low -- and any surge in growth could push it over the edge into inflationary territory, he said.
